name: Bubble Sort
description: Repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are out of order. After each full pass the largest remaining element has settled into its final position, so at most n - 1 passes sort the array.
explanation:
What it is

A comparison sort built entirely from one operation: compare neighbours, swap if they are out of order. Each pass walks the unsorted region once and pushes the largest element to its final slot, like a bubble rising to the surface.

How it works

  1. Compare arr[j] with arr[j + 1] for j from 0 to n - i - 2, swapping when arr[j] > arr[j + 1].
  2. After pass i, the last i elements are in their final positions, so the pass range shrinks by one each time.
  3. Track whether any swap happened during a pass: if none did, the array is already sorted and the algorithm stops early.

Worked example

[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]: pass one gives [1, 4, 2, 5, 8] (8 settled); pass two gives [1, 2, 4, 5, 8] (5 settled); pass three performs no swaps and the flag ends the run. Two passes of a possible four were enough.

Key insight

Bubble sort is stable and in-place, and with the swap flag it runs in O(n) on already-sorted input — but worst and average cases stay O(n²). Its real value is pedagogical: the loop invariants and the swap-per-pass model are the simplest complete picture of a comparison sort.

use: Teaching or visualizing how comparison sorts work
Tiny arrays (a few dozen elements) where simplicity beats constant factors
Nearly sorted data when the early-exit flag is in place
avoid: Any performance-sensitive code — O(n²) is fatal past small n
When a standard library sort is available; use it
Reversed input, where it does the maximum possible swaps

commonMistakes.mistake: The inner loop bound is off by one: writing j < n - i instead of j < n - i - 1 makes arr[j + 1] read into the already-sorted tail, and on the first pass reads past the array entirely.
commonMistakes.fix: Loop j from 0 to n - i - 2 inclusive; the final i elements are already fixed.

commonMistakes.mistake: No early exit: a nearly sorted array still takes all n - 1 passes and roughly n²/2 comparisons, discarding bubble sort's one advantage.
commonMistakes.fix: Set a swapped flag on every swap; if a full pass completes without one, break — the array is sorted.

name: Selection Sort
description: Scans the unsorted region for its minimum and swaps that element into the next sorted slot. It performs at most n - 1 swaps, the fewest of any comparison sort, while always doing Θ(n²) comparisons.
explanation:
What it is

Selection sort grows a sorted prefix one position at a time. For each position it scans the entire remaining suffix to find the smallest element, then swaps that element into place — one swap per pass, regardless of how the array looks.

How it works

  1. For i from 0 to n - 2, scan j from i + 1 to n - 1 tracking the index of the minimum.
  2. After the scan, swap arr[i] with arr[minIndex].
  3. Repeat; the prefix [0..i] is sorted after each pass.

Worked example

[64, 25, 12, 22, 11]: pass one finds 11 and swaps it with 64, giving [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]. Pass two finds 12 and swaps with 25: [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]. After three more passes the array is sorted — 4 swaps for 5 elements.

Key insight

Selection sort does not adapt: it performs the same Θ(n²) comparisons on already-sorted input as on random input. What it controls is writes — exactly n - 1 swaps — which is why it appears in systems where a write is far more expensive than a read, such as flash memory. It is not stable, because the long-distance swap can move equal keys past each other.

use: Writes are much more expensive than reads (EEPROM/flash-style storage)
Small arrays where a predictable Θ(n) swap count is reassuring
Teaching in-place selection with minimal movement
avoid: Nearly sorted data — it cannot exploit existing order
When stability is required
Large arrays; O(n²) comparisons are unavoidable

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping every time a smaller element is found during the scan, instead of swapping once after it. This turns a Θ(n) write count into Θ(n²) writes, destroying the one property selection sort is chosen for.
commonMistakes.fix: Track only the minimum index during the scan; perform a single swap at the end of each outer iteration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting that selection sort is unstable and relying on equal elements keeping their relative order — a long-distance swap silently reorders them.
commonMistakes.fix: If stability matters, use insertion or merge sort; or attach the original position as a tiebreaker key.

name: Insertion Sort
description: Builds a sorted prefix one element at a time: take the next element and shift larger elements right until it fits. Runs in time proportional to the number of inversions, which is why library sorts switch to it for small ranges.
explanation:
What it is

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. Each step takes the next element, walks left while the neighbours are larger, and inserts it into the gap — exactly how most people sort a hand of cards.

How it works

  1. Start at index 1; store the element as key.
  2. Shift every element greater than key one position right (the loop condition must check the index bound before comparing).
  3. Place key in the gap and advance to the next element.

Worked example

[5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]: insert 2 left of 5, giving [2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3]; insert 4 between 2 and 5, giving [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3]; 6 is already in place; 1 shifts everything right; 3 lands between 2 and 4.

Key insight

Insertion sort runs in Θ(n + k) where k is the number of inversions: sorted input costs n comparisons, reversed input about n²/2. That is why real library sorts — TimSort, Introsort — drop to insertion sort below roughly 16–32 elements. It is stable, in-place and online: it can sort elements as they arrive.

use: Small ranges (under a few dozen elements), exactly where hybrid library sorts use it
Nearly sorted data — cost grows with the number of inversions, not n²
Streaming input where elements arrive and must be kept sorted
avoid: Large random or reversed arrays
When a well-tested library sort is one call away

commonMistakes.mistake: Overwriting the element being inserted: shifting arr[j] into arr[j + 1] without first saving arr[i]. The key is destroyed on the first shift.
commonMistakes.fix: Capture key = arr[i] before the shifting loop, then write key into the final gap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ordering the loop condition as arr[j] > key && j >= 0 — in languages that do not short-circuit, or with unsigned indices, this reads index -1.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the bound first: j >= 0 && arr[j] > key, and use a signed index.

name: Merge Sort
description: Divide-and-conquer sort: split the array until runs have one element, then merge sorted runs pairwise. Guarantees O(n log n) in every case and is stable, at the cost of O(n) auxiliary memory.
explanation:
What it is

Merge sort halves the array, sorts each half recursively, and merges two sorted runs into one by repeatedly taking the smaller front element. It is the standard example of divide-and-conquer.

How it works

  1. Split the range at mid = (low + high) // 2 until the range holds a single element.
  2. Merge: walk both sorted runs with two pointers, always emitting the smaller front element.
  3. When one run is exhausted, append the remainder of the other — forgetting this step is the classic bug.

Worked example

[38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] splits into singletons, then merges: [27, 38], [3, 43], [9, 82], [10]; then [3, 27, 38, 43] and [9, 10, 82]; finally [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

Key insight

Time is O(n log n) in best, average and worst cases alike: log n levels of recursion, Θ(n) merging per level. On ties, taking from the left run keeps equal elements in their original order, which makes the sort stable. Its sequential access pattern makes it the natural choice for linked lists and for external sorting of data larger than memory.

use: You need guaranteed O(n log n) with stability (multi-key object sorting)
Linked lists — merging rewires pointers and needs no random access
External sorting of datasets larger than memory
avoid: Memory-tight settings where an in-place sort fits the budget better
Very small arrays, where insertion sort's lower overhead wins

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the leftover tail: the merge loop stops when one run is exhausted, and the remaining elements of the other run are never appended, so values go missing.
commonMistakes.fix: After the main loop, extend the output with the unexhausted run's remainder.

commonMistakes.mistake: Breaking stability by taking from the right run on ties (comparing with strict <). Equal keys then come out in a different order than they went in.
commonMistakes.fix: On ties take from the left run (arr[i] <= arr[j]); stability is then automatic.

name: Quick Sort
description: Partitions the array around a pivot so smaller elements sit left of it and larger ones right, then sorts both sides. Average O(n log n) with the best cache behaviour of any sort; pivot choice decides whether it degrades to O(n²).
explanation:
What it is

Quick sort picks a pivot, rearranges the range so everything smaller sits left and everything larger sits right, places the pivot between the two, and recurses on both sides. The partitioning work happens before the recursive calls, not after.

How it works

  1. Choose a pivot — random or median-of-three, not the first or last element by reflex.
  2. Partition the range (Lomuto: one scan, swap smaller elements forward; Hoare: two pointers moving inward).
  3. Recurse on the left and right subranges, excluding the settled pivot position.

Worked example

[10, 7, 8, 9, 1, 5] with pivot 5 (Lomuto): elements below 5 collect first, giving [1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 7]. The pivot is final at index 1; the right side recurses and finishes in one more pass.

Key insight

With random pivots the expected depth is O(log n) and the sort is the fastest general-purpose comparison sort in practice — small constants, in-place partitioning, and cache-friendly sequential scans. The worst case is O(n²) when the pivot is consistently extreme, which is exactly what happens on sorted input if the pivot is always the last element. Production implementations (Introsort) watch the recursion depth and fall back to heap sort to make O(n log n) a guarantee.

use: General-purpose in-memory sorting of arrays where constant factors and locality matter
When the pivot can be randomized or chosen by median-of-three
Situations tolerant of O(n log n) expected rather than guaranteed time
avoid: Stability required — partitioning is unstable by construction
Adversarial input with a predictable pivot; randomize or use a different sort
When worst-case O(n log n) must be guaranteed (heapsort, merge sort)

commonMistakes.mistake: Lomuto partitioning with a fixed last-element pivot on sorted or constant input: every partition peels off a single element, giving O(n²) time and O(n) recursion depth.
commonMistakes.fix: Randomize the pivot or use median-of-three; with many duplicates, three-way partitioning (Dutch flag) splits equals into their own band.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hoare partition loop bounds wrong: advancing i and j with no guard lets them run past the array ends, producing out-of-range reads or infinite recursion.
commonMistakes.fix: Advance while arr[i] < pivot and arr[j] > pivot, stop when i >= j, and recurse on [low..j] and [j+1..high].

commonMistakes.mistake: Recursing on an empty or single-element range because the base case is missing, or recursing on the full range including the settled pivot — both paths loop forever or touch the wrong interval.
commonMistakes.fix: Base case: return when low >= high. Recurse strictly to the left and right of the final pivot index.

name: Heap Sort
description: Builds a max-heap in the array, then repeatedly moves the root (the maximum) to the end and restores the heap over the remaining part. Guarantees O(n log n) and sorts in place, unlike merge sort, but it is not stable.
explanation:
What it is

Heap sort treats the array itself as a binary tree: index i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and a max-heap satisfies parent >= children everywhere. Building that structure and then dismantling it one maximum at a time sorts the array.

How it works

  1. Build a max-heap: sift down every internal node from floor(n/2) - 1 down to 0. This costs O(n) total, not O(n log n).
  2. Swap the root (current maximum) with the last element of the heap.
  3. Shrink the heap by one and sift the new root down. Repeat until one element remains.

Key insight

Heap sort is the only common comparison sort that offers both a worst-case O(n log n) guarantee and O(1) auxiliary space — the combination that matters in real-time systems. The price is practical speed: sifting jumps around memory, so it loses to quicksort on cache-bound workloads and it cannot preserve stability, since equal keys are separated by long-distance swaps.

use: Worst-case O(n log n) is required with O(1) extra memory
Real-time or embedded contexts where a bounded worst case matters more than average speed
As the safety fallback inside hybrid sorts (Introsort)
avoid: Stability required
Cache-sensitive or latency-tolerant workloads where quicksort simply benchmarks faster

commonMistakes.mistake: Using 1-based child formulas on a 0-based array (children 2i and 2i + 1 instead of 2i + 1 and 2i + 2): sift-down compares the wrong nodes and the heap property silently never holds.
commonMistakes.fix: Commit to the 0-based layout: left = 2i + 1, right = 2i + 2, parent = (i - 1) // 2, and unit-test it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building the heap by sifting down from the last index instead of the last internal node, wasting half the work on leaves that are already valid heaps.
commonMistakes.fix: Start the build loop at floor(n/2) - 1 — the last node that has children.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sifting down over the full array after each extraction instead of the shrinking heap region, so freshly placed sorted elements get pulled back into the heap and the sort never converges.
commonMistakes.fix: Track the heap boundary: after swapping out the root, restore the heap over [0..heapSize - 1] only.

name: Counting Sort
description: Sorts integers by counting how often each value occurs, then turning those counts into starting positions with prefix sums, so every element is placed straight into its final slot. Linear time — but only when the value range stays close to the number of elements.
explanation:
What it is

Counting sort never compares two elements. It treats each value as an address in an auxiliary count array, tallies how often every value appears, converts the tallies into prefix sums, and then writes each element directly to the position computed for it. That escapes the O(n log n) comparison lower bound every comparison sort obeys, but the restriction that pays for it is strict: keys must be small non-negative integers.

How it works

  1. Count: for each value v, increment count[v - min] — the offset makes the array work for any minimum, not just 0.
  2. Prefix sums: replace each count with the number of elements less than or equal to it, so count[v] now marks the end of v's slot band.
  3. Place right to left: walk the input backwards, write each element into its band, and decrement the band pointer. The backwards walk is what keeps equal elements in their original order.

Worked example

[4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1] over values 1-8: the counts are [1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]; the prefix sums give the 2s the slots 1-2 and the 3s the slots 3-4. Placing right to left produces [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8], with both pairs of duplicates still in their original relative order.

Key insight

Time and memory are O(n + k), where k is the size of the value range. When k is O(n) — grades, ages, byte values, small status codes — counting sort is the fastest practical option, and its stability is what makes it the per-digit engine inside radix sort. When k dwarfs n (counting to 10^9 to sort a hundred values), the count array itself becomes the bottleneck, and a comparison sort is the honest choice. No pair of elements is ever compared, so the technique works on any key that can index an array — a shortcut no comparison sort can copy.

use: Integer keys from a small, dense range: grades, ages, byte values, small enum codes
As the stable per-digit pass inside radix sort
When the value range is close to the element count, making O(n + k) effectively linear
avoid: Sparse or huge key ranges — memory scales with the largest value, not the input size
Non-integer or composite keys without a mapping to consecutive integers
In-place requirements: it needs a second array at least as long as the input

commonMistakes.mistake: Off-by-one in the placement pass: treating raw counts as start positions instead of prefix sums, or decrementing after writing instead of before — elements land one slot off and overwrite each other.
commonMistakes.fix: Commit to one convention: prefix sums mark band ends, so decrement the band pointer first and write second; test with duplicate values immediately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Scanning the input left to right during placement. The output still comes out sorted, but equal elements are reversed relative to their input order — the stability radix sort depends on is silently gone.
commonMistakes.fix: Iterate the input right to left so the last equal element lands in the highest slot of its band; assert stability with a tagged (key, value) test case.

commonMistakes.mistake: Indexing the count array with the raw value when the minimum is not 0 (or when negatives appear), reading or writing outside the array.
commonMistakes.fix: Size the array max - min + 1 and index with value - min everywhere; unit-test a range that starts below zero.

name: Shell Sort
description: An insertion sort that first works on elements far apart and keeps halving the gap: early passes remove long-distance disorder cheaply, leaving the final gap-1 pass with almost nothing to do. In place, and fast in practice despite worst-case bounds that took decades to pin down.
explanation:
What it is

Shell sort generalises insertion sort along a gap sequence. Insertion sort is fast when elements sit close to where they belong; sorting every gap-th subsequence first moves elements long distances in single swaps, so each later pass meets a more orderly array. The last pass, gap = 1, is a genuine insertion sort over an almost-sorted array — its best case.

How it works

  1. Pick a gap sequence — halving from n/2 down to 1 is the original; Knuth's 3h + 1 and Ciura's sequence perform measurably better.
  2. For each gap, insertion-sort the subsequences of elements gap apart — one interleaved pass over indices gap..n-1, comparing arr[j] with arr[j - gap].
  3. Shrink the gap until it reaches 1; that final pass guarantees the array is fully sorted.

Worked example

[8, 5, 3, 2, 7, 6, 1, 4] with halving gaps. Gap 4 swaps (8, 7) and (3, 1): [7, 5, 1, 2, 8, 6, 3, 4]. Gap 2 clears most of the rest: [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 5, 8, 6] — every element is now within one move of home. The gap-1 pass moves only 5 and 6: two cheap fixes on an almost-sorted array.

Key insight

Shell sort was the first algorithm to break the quadratic barrier for general inputs, and its complexity is decided almost entirely by the gap sequence: halving has a quadratic worst case, Knuth's 3h + 1 guarantees O(n^1.5), and Ciura's sequence does roughly O(n^1.3) in practice. Because it stays in place and needs no recursion or auxiliary memory, it survives in small embedded C libraries to this day. The trade-off: it is not stable, and no single gap sequence is known to be optimal for every size — pinning down its bounds took decades of analysis.

use: Small, memory-tight codebases: a few lines, in place, no recursion to overflow
Moderate arrays where its low overhead and adaptivity compete with heavier O(n log n) machinery
Teaching incremental sorting: insertion sort plus one scheduling idea
avoid: Stability-sensitive data — the gapped passes reorder equal keys
Hard worst-case guarantees — prefer merge or heap sort when the bound must hold
Large datasets where introsort-style hybrids are simply faster

commonMistakes.mistake: Ending the gap sequence above 1 (for example stopping at 2): the array is then only gap-sorted, not sorted, and the bug looks like a handful of stubborn misplaced elements.
commonMistakes.fix: Every valid gap sequence finishes with 1 — the final pass is the real insertion sort. Assert it in code: gaps[gaps.length - 1] === 1.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing across a gap without the j >= gap bound, so the look-back reads index -gap on the first element of a subsequence.
commonMistakes.fix: Loop while j >= gap and arr[j - gap] > arr[j], shrinking j by gap inside the loop.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming O(n log n) because repeated halving sounds logarithmic: with the halving sequence the worst case is quadratic on adversarial inputs.
commonMistakes.fix: Choose the sequence deliberately (Knuth's 3h + 1 gives O(n^1.5)) and test adversarial patterns — alternating low/high values — not just random arrays.
